docs.title: Lesson 4 — Interpreting and Clearing the Check
docs.text:
Estimated time: 75 minutes

This lesson uses TAMBAB, the Phase B copy of the Tamba New Testament practice project (configured, with five seeded errors). Your mentor gives you access to it before this lesson: receive it with Paratext > Send/Receive projects..., and do all of Lesson 4 in TAMBAB, not in TAMBA, which keeps your own Lesson 2–3 settings. See the mentor guide for how the facilitator stages Phase B.

WARNING: Receive TAMBAB once. After that, never Send/Receive it: your fixes would go to every other learner. Save your work instead; the check runs on your own copy. If Paratext offers to Send/Receive (for example, after a permission change), cancel it.

Purpose: A configured check still produces results — and on a real project the whole value of your work is being able to look at each one and decide, correctly and quickly, whether to fix the text or fix the settings. This lesson is where configuration becomes troubleshooting: reading results, classifying them, and clearing a book to zero without erasing correct Scripture.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Classify a check result as a real error or a configuration problem.
  • Take the correct corrective action for each type.
  • Recognize the rare case where a result is neither — a genuine collision Paratext cannot resolve through configuration — and know what to do with it instead.
  • Work through a result set systematically to reach zero actionable errors.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
By now you have configured TAMBA yourself (Lessons 2 and 3). For this lesson you switch to TAMBAB, the same Tamba text with that configuration already entered. Run the check and you will still see results — but now they mean something. The skill this lesson builds is the judgment call you will make dozens of times on a real project: fix the text, or fix the settings?

✏️ Reflection. Think back to Lesson 1 — the five John 17 results that came from Paratext's default settings rather than from anything wrong in the text, and the team lead who wanted to add closing marks to clear them — and to a project you support:

  • When a check lights up, what is your first instinct — start editing verses, or step back and ask whether the settings are right?
  • What would go wrong if you "fixed" a check result by deleting a quotation mark from correctly translated text?
  • How might you tell, at a glance, whether a batch of similar results is one settings gap or many separate text mistakes?

docs.title: Content
docs.text:
This closes the Translation Tools "use and troubleshoot" loop: you configured the check, now you interpret it. The core discipline is never editing correct text just to make a result disappear — that corrupts the translation to quiet a tool.

After configuration you will typically have two kinds of results:

  1. Real errors — a mark is genuinely missing, extra, or at the wrong level. Fix these in the text.
  2. Configuration problems — the check flags something that reveals a gap in your inventory or rules. Fix these by refining the configuration, not by editing the text.

A rare third case: occasionally a result is neither. When the same character is used as both a Second (or Third) level closing mark and a word-medial apostrophe, Paratext's Word-medial punctuation setting (Language Settings > Other Characters) — which looks built for exactly this — does not actually suppress the resulting "closing quote found as a word medial character" flag, confirmed against real Paratext 9.5 behavior. There is no text fix (the apostrophe is correct) and no configuration fix (the setting doesn't take effect once the character is already a quote mark). The correct action is to verify the flagged instance really is a genuine apostrophe, then leave it and move on — document it for whoever inherits the project rather than losing time hunting for a setting that doesn't exist. You'll meet this exact case in Exercise 4.1, item 5.

The one real fix is upstream of the check entirely: a different, unique character for the apostrophe — Lesson 2 recommends ʼ (U+02BC MODIFIER LETTER APOSTROPHE), the character Unicode itself designates for an apostrophe functioning as a letter rather than as punctuation. That eliminates the collision outright rather than living with documented false positives. But choosing the apostrophe character is an orthography decision, and it belongs to the translation team and the language community, not to a Paratext setting. It can come up late — orthography changes are sometimes made right up to typesetting — so you can raise it whenever the collision appears, but you don't make it. In this course's practice text, leave the apostrophe as written.

Read each result as three parts: the location (book, chapter, verse), the message (what the check thinks is wrong), and the text in context (open the verse and look). A useful heuristic: the same message repeated across many verses usually points to a configuration gap; a one-off result usually points to a real error in that verse.

Key takeaways

  • Almost every result is one of two types: real error (fix the text) or configuration problem (fix the Quote marks tab or Quotation types tab).
  • Never edit correct text to make a result disappear — fix the configuration instead.
  • The one confirmed exception: a quote-mark/apostrophe character collision. Neither fix applies — verify it's genuine, document it, and move on.
  • Work book by book — Matthew first, then expand. A full-NT result list is overwhelming; a single-book list is actionable.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text: The TAMBAB project is Tamba in Phase B: fully configured, but seeded with five deliberate issues. Your job is to triage them correctly, then clear a book to zero. Your filled-in tables and reasoning are what a mentor reviews.

docs.title: Exercise 4.1 — Triage a dirty result set
docs.text:
The TAMBAB project has been seeded with five issues — but the check reports seven results, because one issue (#3) is a single broken mark whose damage is reported back as three separate, differently-worded results at three different verses. This is common: one broken mark in the middle of a long quotation confuses the tracking on both sides of it, so the checker reports the symptom in multiple places even though there is exactly one thing to fix. Before reading further, fill in the Your prediction column for all five rows — write 1 (Real error), 2 (Configuration problem), or 3 (Neither — cannot be resolved through configuration). For row 3, make one prediction that covers all three linked results. Only after you have written a prediction for every row should you read the discovery prompts and open the verses.

# Location Check message Your prediction Actual type 1 Matthew 5:3 "Closing quote mark is possibly missing before verse 7:28" ? ? 2 Luke 4:18 "Closing quote mark is possibly missing before verse 20" ? ? 3 John 3:10, 3:16, 3:21 — one seed, three linked results 3:10: "Quote opened; see following message for error" · 3:16: "Expected continuers [“] are missing OR quote not closed; see preceding message" · 3:21: "Closing quote [” U+201D] found without matching opening. Caused by a missing opening quote, a missing continuer, or incorrectly defined continuer rules" ? ? 4 Acts 2:25 "Opening quote mark found without matching closing quote mark" ? ? 5 Romans 1:1 "Closing quote [’ U+2019] found as a word medial character. Sometimes caused when a closing quote is incorrectly used as an apostrophe" ? ?

✏️ Discovery prompts for each item: - Matthew 5:3 opens Jesus's speech, and the check traces it forward to verse 7:28 — the whole Sermon on the Mount, not just the Beatitudes. Open the span and find every place the First level speech should close: look at 5:12–13 as well as 7:27–28 (7:28 is the narrator again). What closing mark should be there, is it, and what does the check report when it is absent? - Luke 4:18 contains an Isaiah citation. Does Tamba use dialogue marks for narrator scripture citations? If not, what should you do with a stray opening “ before the citation? Notice the check doesn't call this mark "unexpected" — it just treats it as a legitimate new opening and complains that its close is missing, wherever the next real closing mark happens to fall. What does that tell you about how much the checker actually "knows" about your language's conventions? - John 3:10, 3:16, and 3:21 are three separate results, but open the whole span in one sitting. Verse 3:16 begins a new \p paragraph inside Jesus's speech. What character should open a continued paragraph of First level speech in Tamba? If you see a straight " (U+0022) there instead, will the check recognize it as the continuer? Once you spot the one broken mark, ask yourself: does fixing only that one character, then running the check again (close the results panel and run it fresh, not "Rerun"), clear all three results, or just one? - Acts 2:25–28: Peter cites Psalm 16 in Second level marks, opening with ‘ in 2:25, as one continuous span across several paragraph breaks. Tamba's Second level has no continuer, and TAMBA (Phase A) passes the check with this span unbroken — so the paragraph breaks are not the problem. Where should the citation close, and is the closing mark there? - Romans 1:1 has no dialogue. How could ’ (U+2019) inside a word cause the check to report a quotation problem? Try the fix Lesson 2 taught for this exact situation (Word-medial punctuation in Language Settings) and re-run the check with a genuinely fresh run, not just "Rerun" on the open panel. Does the result actually clear?

Expected resolution (answer key):

# Actual type Action 1 Real error Add the missing ” (U+201D) in two places: in Matthew 5:12, where Jesus's speech (opened with “ U+201C at 5:3) closes before it reopens with “ at the start of 5:13, and in 7:27, where the speech closes before the narrator resumes at 7:28 (7:28 has no quote marks). Both closing marks were deleted; the check reports the unclosed speech once, at its opening verse 5:3, tracing forward to 7:28. Add both, then re-run. 2 Real error Delete the stray “ (U+201C) before the Isaiah citation in Luke 4:18. Tamba does not mark narrator scripture citations; the mark was added by mistake. 3 Real error (one fix, three results) Verse 3:16 begins a new \p paragraph inside Jesus's speech, so it should open with Tamba's First level Quote Continuer “ (U+201C) — but a straight " (U+0022) sits there instead. That single wrong character is what produces all three results: the check doesn't recognize it as the continuer, so it reports the speech as "opened" at 3:10 (where it actually starts), reports the missing continuer at 3:16, and then reports the speech's closing ” at 3:21 as orphaned, with nothing left to match against. Replace the " at the start of 3:16 with “ (U+201C), re-run the check, and all three results — 3:10, 3:16, and 3:21 — clear together. Do not chase 3:10 or 3:21 individually; there is nothing wrong at those verses themselves. 4 Real error Add the missing closing ’ (U+2019) in 2:28 that ends Peter's Psalm 16 citation. The citation opens with ‘ (U+2018) in 2:25 and runs as one Second level span across several paragraph breaks; that is valid under Tamba's configuration (Second level has no continuer, and Phase A passes the check with the span unbroken), so don't add close/reopen pairs at the breaks. Only the closing mark is missing. 5 Neither — confirmed unresolvable The ’ (U+2019) in Romans 1:1 is a genuine apostrophe inside a word, which Paratext reads as the Second level closing mark with no matching opener. Adding ’ to ☰ > Project settings > Language Settings > Other Characters > Word-medial punctuation looks like the fix (and is what Lesson 2 teaches), but confirmed against real Paratext 9.5 behavior, it does not suppress this result — the check keeps flagging it even after the setting is saved and a fully fresh check is run. There is no text change to make either (the apostrophe is correct as written). Verify the character really is a word-medial apostrophe, then leave the result and move on; note it for anyone else who picks up this project so they don't re-attempt the same fix.

docs.title: Exercise 4.2 — Reach zero actionable errors
docs.text:
Goal: Work through the full result list for the TAMBAB project until every result has either been cleared (by fixing the text or adjusting the configuration) or, for the one confirmed unresolvable case, verified and documented as an expected false positive. "Zero actionable errors" does not mean a literal zero-length results list once Romans is in scope — it means nothing left in the list still needs your action.

NOTE: In this exercise, "re-run" means a full re-run: close the results panel, then run the check again (☰ > Tools > Run basic checks...). Clicking Rerun on the panel that is already open does not pick up your text changes. It keeps showing the old results, so a correct fix looks as if it failed.

Steps: 1. Limit the scope to Matthew first. Work that book to zero results before expanding — Matthew has no unresolvable cases, so a true zero is the right target there. 2. Work through the results top-to-bottom. 3. For each result: open the verse, classify it, take the appropriate action. - Real error: edit the verse text to fix the mark, then close the results panel and run the check again. - Configuration problem: adjust the Quote marks tab or Quotation types tab, then close the results panel and run the check again. Do not edit the text to make marks disappear — fix the configuration instead. - Neither (confirmed unresolvable): a quote-mark/apostrophe collision, like Romans 1:1. Verify the flagged character is genuinely a word-medial apostrophe, then leave it — do not keep trying configuration changes to clear it, and do not edit the text. 4. After fixing a batch of real errors, close the results panel and run the check again from Run basic checks to confirm the count drops. 5. Once Matthew is clean, expand the scope one book at a time through the NT. When you reach Romans, expect the count to stop at 1 (the 1:1 apostrophe) rather than reaching 0 — that remaining result is correct, not a sign something is still wrong. 6. When unsure whether a result is a real error or a configuration problem, look at how often the same message appears: the same message repeated across many verses usually points to a configuration gap; a one-off result usually points to a real error in that verse. 7. Watch for linked results: a cluster of different messages at nearby verses — typically an "opened"/"quote opened" message, followed by an "expected continuer" or "not closed" message, followed by an orphaned "closing mark found without matching opening" further on — usually traces back to one broken mark in the middle of the chain, not three separate errors. Fix the one mark, close the results panel and run the check again, and confirm the whole cluster clears together before treating any of the other verses in the cluster as needing their own fix.

Completion criteria: - The Quotations check shows 0 results for every book except Romans. - Romans shows exactly 1 result (the 1:1 apostrophe), verified as a genuine word-medial apostrophe and documented rather than chased with further configuration changes.

✏️ Produce this (a mentor will review it). Submit your completed triage table (predictions + actual types) and a one-line note for each result on the action you took and why. The point a mentor is checking is your reasoning — that you fixed text only for real errors and settings only for configuration problems.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
Self-assessment — can you explain it to a colleague?

  1. Two results appear in Luke 22: "Quote opened; see following message for error" at 22:35, and "Expected continuers [“] are missing OR quote not closed; see preceding message" at 22:36. Jesus is speaking from verse 35 through verse 38, where the speech closes with the final ”. What type of result is this, and what should you do?
  2. You have cleared all real errors in Matthew but 6 results remain. The translation team has looked at those verses and confirmed the text is as they intend it. What should you do next?
  3. In Romans 8:1, a verse with no dialogue, the check reports "Second-level quote mark found without a preceding first-level quote: ‘". What is the most likely cause and correct action?

You should be able to say: (1) This is the same linked pattern as John 3:10 and 3:16 in Exercise 4.1: an "opened" message pointing to a following one. Open 22:35–38 in one sitting. If 22:36 begins a new paragraph inside the speech, Tamba's First level Quote Continuer “ should open it. If it is missing, or a look-alike such as a straight " sits there instead, that one mark is a real error: put in the “ (U+201C), close the results panel, run the check again, and both results should clear together. (2) Once the team has confirmed the text, the remaining results are about the settings, not the text — review each to find the missing rule or setting (e.g. a Quotation types setting that doesn't match how the language uses marks there), adjust, and re-run until they clear. If any of them is the apostrophe collision from Lesson 2, that is the third case: verify it and document it. (3) Most likely a stray opening ‘ with no First level speech around it, perhaps copied from a source text. This is not the Romans 1:1 case: that message was about ’ inside a word, and this one is about an opening ‘. Open the verse and find the mark. A stray mark is a real error — a text correction, not a configuration change — so confirm with the translation team that it doesn't belong, then remove it.

✏️ Take it to your context. Recall a real check result you (or a translator you support) have seen. Would you now classify it as a real error or a configuration problem — and what would you have done differently knowing the two-type distinction?

Next step. You have taken one language, Tamba, from Paratext's default settings to zero actionable errors. The scenario bank puts the full workflow — inventory → rules → check → triage — to work on three unfamiliar languages (Velna, Menda, Waku), each with its own conventions and edge cases.

Previous: Lesson 3 — Configuring Quotation Types · Next: Scenario Bank — Language Scenario Practice

docs.title: Scenario Bank — Language Scenario Practice
docs.text:
Estimated time: 90 minutes

Three independent scenarios, roughly 30 minutes each. Scenarios A and B are core practice; Scenario C (Waku em-dash) is an optional stretch for learners who complete A and B confidently. Do them in any order. Each uses its own practice project — see the mentor guide for how the facilitator distributes them.

Learning objectives: By the end of this scenario bank you will be able to apply the complete inventory + rules + check + triage workflow independently to an unfamiliar language scenario, including edge cases not covered in Lessons 1–4.

These exercises use three new practice projects. Each has a different quotation style, and each starts where a real new project starts: with Paratext's default Quotation Rules, not the language's conventions. For each scenario follow the same four-step workflow — inventory → rules → check → triage — broken into eight concrete actions:

Inventory

  1. Read the language conventions table.
  2. Run the Quotations check on all books once, before changing anything, and note what it reports. Then answer the discovery prompts.
  3. Open the Quote marks tab and compare every cell with the conventions table. It holds Paratext's defaults (“ “ ” at First level, ‘ ‘ ’ at Second level, “ “ ” at Third level, Continuer required at p p/q1 b/q1).
  4. Correct the defaults: change every cell that differs, including continuers and unused levels that must be set to none, and the Continuer required at list.

Rules

  1. Configure the Quotation types tab.

Check

  1. Run the check (start with one book).

Triage

  1. Triage the results to zero actionable errors.
  2. Compare your configuration against the expected answer key.

docs.title: Scenario A — Guillemet (French style)
docs.text:
Project: Velna New Testament (VELNA)

Velna quotation conventions:

Level Opening Unicode Closing Unicode First level « U+00AB » U+00BB Second level ‘ U+2018 ’ U+2019

No Third level. First level opening mark « also appears at the start of continued paragraphs.

Starting state: Paratext's defaults. Run the Quotations check on all books before you change anything: it reports 264 results. Most read "Second-level quote mark found without a preceding first-level quote: ‘"; there are also "Closing quote [ ’ U+2019 ] found as a word medial character" results (Matthew 1:1, for example).

Discovery prompts: - Most of the 264 results say a Second level ‘ has no First level quote around it. Velna's conventions use ‘ only inside «…» speech. What does that tell you about whether the check can see Velna's First level marks at the defaults? Is it the text or the settings that needs attention? - Velna uses ’ (U+2019) as both its Second level closing mark and as an apostrophe. Try adding ’ to Word-medial punctuation as Lesson 2 taught — does it actually clear the resulting check result here too? - How would you verify that the text contains « (U+00AB) rather than << (two less-than signs)?

Expected configuration:

Level Opening Quote Continuer at new paragraph Closing First level « « » Second level ‘ none ’ Third level none none none

What changes from the defaults: all three First level cells (“ “ ” → « « »); the Second level continuer, which must be cleared from ‘ to none; and all three Third level cells, which must be cleared from “ “ ” to none, because Velna has no Third level. The Second level Opening ‘ and Closing ’ already match.

Continuation: « at First level only. The verified configuration also replaces the default Continuer required at list (p p/q1 b/q1) with p b/q1 pi pi/pi — the paragraph-marker contexts where the check must insist on the continuer. Copy it exactly; without the right list the check reads continuers « as new opening marks that are never closed, and a long speech floods with unclosed-quote results.

Word-medial punctuation: add ’ (U+2019) in ☰ > Project settings > Language Settings > Other Characters tab > Word-medial punctuation — do this anyway, since it's the correct habit to build, but confirmed on a real Paratext 9.5 build, it will not stop the check from flagging Velna's word-medial apostrophes. That's expected: once ’ is already a configured quote mark, this setting has no effect on it. You will also see the same yellow warning triangle (⚠) Lesson 2 Exercise 2.3 showed you, in both dialogs: at the end of the Word-medial punctuation field and in the Second level Closing cell on the Quote marks tab, each with the hover message described there. That is expected too; click OK anyway. Treat any remaining apostrophe results as verified false positives, not something left to configure away. This is also the moment to remember the real fix: on a live translation team's project, you would raise with the team adopting a different, unique apostrophe character — Lesson 2 names ʼ (U+02BC MODIFIER LETTER APOSTROPHE) as a concrete option — rather than living with the collision indefinitely. Choosing it is an orthography decision for the translation team and the language community, not for you, and it can come up late, even close to typesetting. Velna itself keeps ’ for its apostrophes so the scenario still demonstrates the unresolvable case firsthand; the ʼ alternative is illustrated in Lesson 2's text, not built into this project.

Quotation types tab: confirmed on a real Paratext 9.5 build: Velna needs exactly one change from recommended defaults — Continued quotation = Use quote marks (the First level continuer means a mark is expected at every continued paragraph, same reasoning as Tamba in Lesson 3). Unlike Tamba, Velna has no narrator-citation, self-quote, or indirect-speech exceptions, so every other type — Normal, Quotation from another source, Self quote, Potential, Indirect, Hypothetical — stays at its recommended default.

Check your work: - After configuration, run the check on all books again and compare with the 264 you started from. Read the messages, not just the count: which kinds of result has your configuration cleared, and which are left? - Run the check on Luke. Verify that «...» speech boundaries are recognized correctly and narrative passages generate no results. - Confirm that apostrophes inside words (contractions, possessives) are still flagged even after configuring Word-medial punctuation — that's the expected, confirmed outcome for this collision, not a sign of a missing setting. Verify each is a genuine apostrophe and move on. - Confirm the First level Quote Continuer («) at the start of continued paragraphs is not flagged as an unexpected mark. - Enable the Quotation types check and run it on Matthew, Luke, and John. It should return clean once Continued quotation is set to Use quote marks — this check is separate from the apostrophe results above, which live in the Quotations check and remain regardless.

docs.title: Scenario B — Angle-bracket guillemets (French/German style with nesting reversal)
docs.text:
Project: Menda New Testament (MENDA)

Menda quotation conventions:

Level Opening Unicode Closing Unicode First level « U+00AB » U+00BB Second level › U+203A ‹ U+2039 Third level « U+00AB » U+00BB

Note: At Second level Menda uses single guillemets in reversed order — the › (U+203A, right-pointing) opens the embedded speech and ‹ (U+2039, left-pointing) closes it. This is unusual and easy to get wrong.

At Third level Menda returns to double guillemets — « opens and » closes, the same characters as First level. Third level is rare; John 19:21 is the key example.

Starting state: Paratext's defaults. Run the Quotations check on all books before you change anything: it reports "No errors found."

Discovery prompts: - Menda's text is full of dialogue, and the check at the defaults says "No errors found." Why isn't that good news? Which of Menda's quote marks appear anywhere in Paratext's default grid? - Why might it be confusing that the opening mark for Second level is the right-pointing single guillemet? What would happen if you entered it in the Closing field by mistake? - How would you verify which direction the single guillemet in the text actually points? (Hint: open the Punctuation inventory or the Characters inventory. Select a single guillemet in the upper pane to see its Unicode value, 203A or 2039. The lower pane lists the verses where it occurs, and in short verses you can see both marks of the pair. Or place the cursor just after the character and press Alt+X (Edit > Show/hide Unicode) to show its code, then press Alt+X again to switch it back.) - If a verse shows «Il a dit ‹oui›» and the check flags Second level as having incorrect marks, what is the most likely cause? - John 19:21 nests speech three levels deep. What characters does Menda use at the Third level, and what might the check report at 19:21 if the Third level cells are left at the defaults?

Expected configuration:

Level Opening Quote Continuer at new paragraph Closing First level « none » Second level › none ‹ Third level « none »

What changes from the defaults: every cell. The six Opening and Closing cells change from the default curly quotes to guillemets, and all three continuer cells, which default to “, ‘ and “, must be cleared to none. The Continuer required at list changes too: clear it from p p/q1 b/q1 to empty. None of Menda's marks are in the defaults, which is why the check at the defaults recognized no quote marks at all and reported "No errors found."

Continuer required at: empty. Menda has no continuer at any level, so the list has nothing to require; set it to what the conventions say. Do it in this order: set all three continuers to none first, then clear the list. Paratext won't accept an empty list while any continuer is still set: a red ! appears beside the field, its tooltip reads "Cannot be blank if any Quote Continuer is specified.", and OK is disabled.

Continuation: none. Apostrophe handling: not needed — Menda's Quote marks tab does not use U+2019, so no Word-medial punctuation setting is required.

Quotation types tab: unlike Tamba (Lesson 3), Menda needs no customization at all — leave it on Use recommended settings. Confirmed on a real Paratext 9.5 build: with the Quotation types check enabled, Menda's text passes clean at the recommended defaults (Normal/Quotation from another source/Self quote = Use quote marks; Continued quotation = Never use quote marks; Potential/Indirect = Quote marks are optional; Hypothetical = Never use quote marks). Step 5 of the scenario workflow still applies — open the tab, tick the enable checkbox, and verify with a check run — but for Menda that verification is the whole task; there is nothing to change.

Check your work: - Run the check on John (contains clear nested dialogue). Verify that «...›...‹...» structures pass without errors. - If the check fires on every Second level opening mark, the Opening and Closing fields for Second level are likely reversed. Confirm which character is right-pointing (›) and which is left-pointing (‹). - After entering Second level, check the Example section at the bottom. If › opens and ‹ closes in the example, you have the correct order. The visual difference between › and ‹ is easy to miss — use the Example to confirm before clicking OK. - John 19:21 contains Menda's rare Third level quotation. Verify it passes once Third level is configured — if 19:21 is flagged, check that the Third level cells really hold « and », not the default “ and ”. - Enable the Quotation types check and run it on John. It should return clean at recommended settings with no customization — if it doesn't, re-check your Quote marks tab entries first, since a character-level mistake there is more likely than a genuine need to customize types.

docs.title: Scenario C — Non-standard marks with continuation
docs.text:
Project: Waku New Testament (Waku)

Waku quotation conventions:

Level Opening Unicode Closing Unicode First level — U+2014 — U+2014 Second level “ U+201C ” U+201D Third level ‘ U+2018 ’ U+2019

Waku uses an em dash (U+2014) for both the opening and closing mark at First level. Multi-paragraph speech does not restart the em dash — it uses a continuation mark of — (another em dash) at the start of each continued paragraph. Waku's word-medial apostrophe is ʼ (U+02BC MODIFIER LETTER APOSTROPHE), so the Third level closer ’ (U+2019) creates no apostrophe collision.

Starting state: Paratext's defaults. Run the Quotations check on all books before you change anything: like Menda, it reports "No errors found."

Discovery prompts: - Waku's Second and Third level marks are the same curly quotes that appear in Paratext's defaults, and the check at the defaults reports "No errors found." Does that mean the defaults are close enough? What does the default grid say about Waku's First level em dash? - When the same character is used for both opening and closing, how does Paratext know which is which? What rule does it rely on? - Waku uses the em dash as a continuation mark. Should the continuation mark be a different character from the opening mark, or can it be the same character? What happens if they are the same? - In a language where em dash is also used for parenthetical remarks (not speech), how would you expect the check to behave? Is there a way to address this?

Expected configuration:

Level Opening Quote Continuer at new paragraph Closing First level — — — Second level “ none ” Third level ‘ none ’

What changes from the defaults: all three First level cells (“ “ ” → — — —); the Second level Opening and Closing (‘ ’ → “ ”) and its continuer, which must be cleared from ‘ to none; and the Third level Opening and Closing (“ ” → ‘ ’) and its continuer, which must be cleared from “ to none.

Continuation: — (em dash, same character) at First level only. The verified configuration also replaces the default Continuer required at list (p p/q1 b/q1) with p p/q1 b/q1 m/q1 — the paragraph-marker contexts where the check must insist on the continuer. Copy it exactly; without it the check does not enforce the continuer at those paragraph breaks.

Don't stop at the marks. If you change only the Opening and Closing marks and leave the Second and Third level continuers filled in (as the defaults have them) and the default list in place, the check gives an eighth result on top of the seven described below: Matthew 13:14, "Second-level quote mark found without a preceding first-level quote: “". With the full configuration above, that result goes and seven remain.

Note on same-character open/close: When the same character serves as both opener and closer, Paratext relies on structural context (paragraph markers, verse boundaries, and surrounding text flow) to determine which role the em dash plays. Because this context-based interpretation may not resolve every case unambiguously, human review of flagged em-dash results is always required for Waku.

Check your work: - Run the check on Acts (extended speeches, heavy use of em-dash dialogue). Verify that multi-paragraph speeches with continuation marks do not generate "unclosed quote" errors. - Check a verse where em dash is used for a parenthetical aside (not speech). Does the check flag it? What is the correct response — reconfigure if possible, or document it in a Project Note and raise the punctuation question with the translation team? (Changing the text is not your call; see below.) - This scenario leaves results that cannot be eliminated by configuration alone — because Paratext cannot distinguish an em dash used as speech from one used as a parenthetical dash. Confirmed on a real Paratext 9.5 build, a correct configuration run against all books ends at seven results: six "found as a word medial character" results on genuine parenthetical em dashes (Mark 13:14 twice, 13:19, 13:22; Luke 9:3; Acts 3:1), plus one "Closing quote mark is possibly missing before verse 18.1: —" at John 17:26. - The John 17:26 result is a different residual class from the parentheticals: the text there is correct — Jesus's prayer (17:1–26) opens with —, carries the — continuer at every paragraph, and closes with — at the end of verse 26 — but with the same character serving as opener, closer, and continuer across a long multi-paragraph speech, Paratext's context-based tracking loses the open/close state and reports the speech as possibly unclosed. No text change fixes it without breaking Waku's convention. Verify the marks are all present, then document. - For all seven: add a Project Note (☰ > Insert > Project note...) explaining the result, so the consultant can verify it during review. Attach each note to the verse the result is reported at: Mark 13:14, 13:19, 13:22, Luke 9:3, Acts 3:1 and John 17:26. For the six parentheticals, also raise the punctuation question with the translation team: the same em dash marks both speech and parenthetical remarks, so the check can't tell them apart. Whether to change the text, for example by using different punctuation for parentheticals, is the team's decision, not yours. John 17:26 needs no question for the team: its marks are already correct.

docs.title: Scenario bank summary
docs.text:
• The same four-step workflow (inventory → rules → check → triage) applies to every language, however unusual its quotation conventions.
  • Every project starts from Paratext's defaults, and the defaults can mislead in either direction: 264 results for Velna, "No errors found" for Menda and Waku. Correct every cell to the conventions, including the ones that must become none, before you trust any result.
  • Always verify entered characters using the Example section at the bottom of the Quote marks tab — on unfamiliar languages it is easy to confuse visually similar characters.
  • Some languages (like Waku) will always require human review of residual results; zero configuration errors does not always mean zero results.

docs.title: Scenario check-your-understanding
docs.text:
1. You enter Second level Opening as ‹ and Second level Closing as › for the Menda project, then run the check and find that every Second level opening mark generates a result. The Example section in the Quote marks tab shows the marks in reversed order from what you expect. What went wrong, and what is the fix?
  2. In Scenario B you enter Second level as Opening: U+2039, Closing: U+203A (reversed from the correct order). What will the check report?
  3. After completing Scenario C (Waku), 7 results remain in the Basic Checks panel — six em dashes used as parenthetical remarks (not speech), plus one "possibly missing" result on a multi-paragraph speech whose marks are all correctly in place. Configuration cannot eliminate them. What are your options?

Answers

  1. The characters were entered in the wrong fields — the left-pointing guillemet (‹, U+2039) is in the Opening field when it should be in the Closing field, and vice versa. Swap them: Opening should be › (right-pointing, U+203A), Closing should be ‹ (left-pointing, U+2039). Confirm by checking the Example section — the correct order shows › as the inner opening and ‹ as the inner closing.
  2. The check will fire on every Second level opening mark (treating the right-pointing guillemet as an unexpected closing mark) and on every Second level closing mark (treating the left-pointing guillemet as an unexpected opening mark). The entire Second level configuration will appear as errors.
  3. Document all seven with a Project Note (☰ > Insert > Project note...) explaining the result, attached to the verse it is reported at (Mark 13:14, 13:19, 13:22, Luke 9:3, Acts 3:1, John 17:26), so the consultant can verify it during review. The Basic Checks panel results will remain; documenting them prevents them from being mistaken for unreviewed errors. For the six parentheticals, also raise the punctuation question with the translation team: their em dash marks both speech and parenthetical remarks, and the check can't tell the two apart. Whether to change the text, for example by using different punctuation for parentheticals, is the team's decision; you don't rewrite the verses. The John 17:26 result needs only the note, since its marks are already correct.

docs.title: How the Quotation check fits in the Paratext checking workflow
docs.text:
The Quotation check is one of the Basic Checks in Paratext 9.5 (run via ☰ > Tools > Run basic checks...). Basic Checks are typically run and cleared before a book moves to Consultant Check (CC). A consultant reviewer will re-run the checks during review, so the goal is a configuration that genuinely models the language — not a result list emptied by erasing correct text.

The recommended sequence for a book heading toward CC:

  1. Run all Basic Checks (Quotations, Characters, Markers, Footnotes, and others).
  2. Clear each check to zero actionable results by fixing text errors and refining the configuration, verifying that every remaining result is a known false positive.
  3. Where a residual result cannot be cleared by configuration (see Scenario C), document it with a Project Note so the consultant can verify it quickly.

The Quotation check does not need to be perfect before work continues, but it must be clean before CC begins.

docs.title: Maintaining the configuration over time
docs.text:
Quotation Rules are set once per project and persist across sessions, but they need attention when:

  • New text is added. Re-run the check after each significant drafting session; new text may introduce new errors.
  • A new translator joins. Check whether they are typing the same quote-mark characters as the rest of the team. Open the Punctuation inventory, select a quote mark in the upper pane to see its Unicode value, and look in the lower pane for the verses where it occurs; a look-alike, such as a straight " (U+0022) where the conventions use “ (U+201C), shows up as a separate entry. If you find one, raise it with the team; a find-and-replace on the new chapters may be what they decide to do.
  • A new book is started. Some books (like Psalms, Proverbs, or Revelation) have different poetry/prose ratios. Re-run the check after completing the first draft to confirm that poetry lines (\q, \q2) are not generating false quotation results.

docs.title: Copying Quotation Rules to another project
docs.text:
If your language has more than one translation project (for example, a study Bible alongside the main translation), you do not need to reconfigure the Quote marks tab from scratch. Paratext 9.5 can copy settings from a base project:

Open ☰ > Project settings > Quotation Rules on the destination project. At the bottom of the dialog, click Copy quote mark settings... and select the already-configured project as the source. It copies the quote marks but not the Continuer required at list, so type that by hand; otherwise the destination keeps the list it already had (on a new project, the default p p/q1 b/q1). Review every field after copying — differences in verse structure or text conventions between the two projects may require adjustments.

docs.title: What a well-configured project looks like
docs.text:
A project with correctly configured Quotation Rules will:

  • Return zero results in purely narrative passages with no speech.
  • Have every result on an apostrophe or possessive verified as a genuine apostrophe and documented as a known false positive (where ’ is also a quote mark, no setting removes these).
  • Flag only genuine mismatches — missing marks, extra marks, wrong-level marks — in speech sections.
  • Have any residual results (where the same character serves two linguistic purposes and configuration cannot distinguish them) documented in Project Notes (☰ > Insert > Project note...) so a consultant reviewer can verify them without asking for clarification.

Reaching that state is what this course has prepared you to do.

docs.title: Assessment Quiz — Configuring Quotation Rules in Paratext
Assessment quiz (20 questions)
docs.text: This quiz covers all five lessons of the course, including the scenario bank. You need 80% (16/20) to pass. Questions are a mix of recall, scenario-based application, and true/false. Everything asked here is drawn directly from the lessons — work them first.

docs.title: Section 1: What the Quotation Check Does (Questions 1-3)
docs.text:
Question 1: Which two inputs must be configured before the Quotations check can produce trustworthy results? - A) Language Settings and its Other Characters tab - B) The book scope and the Quotations tick box in Run basic checks - C) The Quote marks tab and the Quotation types tab - D) The Example preview and the Copy quote mark settings button

Question 2: TAMBA is still at Paratext's default Quotation Rules. The Quotations check on all books reports five results in John 17, each "Opening quote mark found without matching closing quote mark: “". The team lead asks whether they should add the closing marks. What do you tell them? - A) Yes; five unclosed speeches in one chapter are real errors in the text - B) Not yet; these are still Paratext's settings, so correct those first - C) Yes, but only after the Quotation types check has been enabled too - D) No; delete the five opening marks instead, so no speech is left open

Question 3: True or False: On a project still at Paratext's default Quotation Rules, the Quotations check can report a handful of plausible results, a flood of results, or "No errors found", and none of these can be trusted until the settings match the team's conventions. - A) True - B) False

docs.title: Section 2: Setting Up Quote Marks (Questions 4-8)
docs.text:
Question 4: Runda's conventions have no Third level, but its Quote marks tab still holds Paratext's defaults at Third level (“ “ ”). What do you do with the Third level cells? - A) Leave the defaults; an unused level produces no results - B) Change them to « « », so they match Runda's First level - C) Change them to ‘ ‘ ’, so they match Runda's Second level - D) Set all three Third level cells, Continuer included, to none

Question 5: Correcting TAMBA's defaults, you start by adding pi/pi to the Continuer required at field, click OK and run the Quotations check on all books. The five John 17 results are gone and the check reports "No errors found". Nothing else on the Quote marks tab has been changed yet. What do you do? - A) Set the Second and Third level continuers to none; the clean run shows the list is complete - B) Complete the list to Tamba's six entries; the default continuer cells cause no results in its text - C) Set every level's continuer to none, then type Tamba's full six-entry list into the field - D) Set the Second and Third level continuers to none, then type Tamba's six-entry list

Question 6: On the Quote marks tab you have changed every cell that differed from the team's conventions. Before clicking OK, what is the recommended way to confirm you picked the right characters? - A) Check the sample text in the Example section at the bottom of the dialog - B) Hover each column label and read the character named in the status bar - C) Compare the shapes in the grid with the marks in the convention table - D) Click OK, then run the check on the whole NT and compare the counts

Question 7: On RUNDA you correct the First level cells to « « » but leave the Continuer required at list at the default p p/q1 b/q1. The check on Matthew reports "Expected continuers [«] are missing" at Matthew 2:6 and 4:6, both poetry quoted inside speech. What does this point to, and what is the fix? - A) The list is too long: replace it with just p, then run the check again - B) The list is too short: add q1 as well, then run the check again - C) The continuer cell is at fault: clear First level's continuer, then run again - D) The text is missing continuers: add « before both poems, then run again

Question 8: Runda uses ’ (U+2019) as its Second level closing mark and also as an apostrophe inside words such as don’t, and the check flags those apostrophes as word-medial closing quotes. You add ’ to ☰ > Project settings > Language Settings > Other Characters > Word-medial punctuation, click OK, close the results panel and run the check again. What happens? - A) The word-medial apostrophe results are gone from the new run - B) Paratext won't save the setting, because ’ is already a quote mark - C) Every word-medial apostrophe result is still reported, as before - D) Those results clear, but every Second level ’ is now flagged instead

docs.title: Section 3: Configuring Quotation Types (Questions 9-11)
docs.text:
Question 9: Tamba repeats its First level opening mark “ (U+201C) at the head of each paragraph when a speech runs on. The recommended setting for Continued quotation is Never use quote marks. With the Quotation types check enabled, what should you do? - A) Leave it; Continued quotation applies only to Second and Third level speech - B) Choose Custom settings and set Continued quotation to Use quote marks - C) Leave it, and clear the First level continuer cell on the Quote marks tab - D) Leave it; the continuer cell on the Quote marks tab overrides this setting

Question 10: The Tamba team tells you that when the narrator reports what someone said ("He told them that the harvest was near"), they write it as plain narrative text, and that is how every such verse should stay. The recommended setting for Indirect is Quote marks are optional. What do you do? - A) Leave Indirect at Optional; with no marks in the text, there is nothing for it to flag - B) Choose Custom settings and set Indirect to Use quote marks, so each verse is checked - C) Leave Indirect at Optional, which flags any mark a translator adds to reported speech - D) Choose Custom settings and set Indirect to Never use quote marks

Question 11: You have switched Tamba's Quotation types tab to Custom settings to change three types. The team confirms that a self-quote must be marked just like any other direct speech. Self quote currently shows Use quote marks. What do you do with it? - A) Change it to Quote marks are optional, the safer choice on a custom tab - B) Change it to Never use quote marks, since Normal already checks direct speech - C) Leave it at Use quote marks, and go on to the three types that need changing - D) Change it to Quote marks are optional and note each self-quote for the consultant

docs.title: Section 4: Interpreting and Clearing the Check (Questions 12-17)
docs.text:
Question 12: TAMBAB is configured with the Lesson 2–3 settings, including Quotation from another source = Quote marks are optional. The check reports at Luke 4:18: "Closing quote mark is possibly missing before verse 20". Tamba does not mark narrator scripture citations, and you find a “ (U+201C) immediately before the Isaiah citation in 4:18. How do you classify and handle this result? - A) Real error: add a closing ” (U+201D) before verse 20, where the check points - B) Real error: delete the stray “ (U+201C) before the citation in 4:18 - C) Configuration problem: set Quotation from another source to Use quote marks - D) Neither: leave the result and document it with a Project Note at 4:18

Question 13: In TAMBAB, three results appear together. John 3:10: "Quote opened; see following message for error". John 3:16: "Expected continuers [“] are missing OR quote not closed; see preceding message". John 3:21: "Closing quote [” U+201D] found without matching opening. Caused by a missing opening quote, a missing continuer, or incorrectly defined continuer rules". Verse 3:16 starts a new \p paragraph inside Jesus's speech and begins with a straight " (U+0022). What do you do? - A) Replace the " at 3:16 with ‘ (U+2018), close the results panel and run the check again - B) Add " (U+0022) as the First level continuer on the Quote marks tab, then run the check again - C) Replace the " at 3:16 with “ (U+201C), and add an opening “ before the ” at 3:21 - D) Replace the " at 3:16 with “ (U+201C), close the results panel and run the check again

Question 14: You have fixed every real error the check found in Matthew, but six results remain. All six read "Opening quote mark found without matching closing quote mark: “", each at a different verse, and the translation team confirms the marks in those verses are written the way they intend. What is your next step? - A) Treat them as a configuration problem: find and adjust the setting - B) Classify them as Neither: leave all six and add a Project Note to each - C) Remove the flagged marks from those verses so that Matthew reaches zero - D) Leave Matthew as it is and expand the scope to the rest of the NT

Question 15: You start Exercise 4.2 in TAMBAB, working the result list toward zero actionable errors. How do you scope the check? - A) Run all NT books at once, so no result is missed before you start fixing - B) Start with Romans, so the known exception is dealt with first - C) Run Matthew alone until it is clean, then add one book at a time - D) Start with whichever book shows the most results in a full NT run

Question 16: In TAMBAB, you add the two missing ” (U+201D) marks at Matthew 5:12 and 7:27, then click Rerun on the results panel that is still open. The Matthew 5:3 result "Closing quote mark is possibly missing before verse 7:28" is still listed. What do you do next? - A) Undo the two edits, since the result shows they did not fix the problem - B) Keep looking for another missing ” between Matthew 5:3 and 7:28 - C) Close the results panel and run the check again from Run basic checks - D) Check the Continuer required at list, since the text is now correct

Question 17: Expanding TAMBAB book by book, every book now shows 0 results except Romans, which shows one, at 1:1: "Closing quote [’ U+2019] found as a word medial character. Sometimes caused when a closing quote is incorrectly used as an apostrophe". The verse has no dialogue, and the flagged ’ sits between two letters of a word. When is Romans finished? - A) Once adding ’ to Word-medial punctuation has cleared the result - B) Once the ’ is verified as an apostrophe and the result documented - C) Once the ’ is taken out of the word so that Romans shows 0 results - D) Once the translation team has rewritten 1:1 without the apostrophe

docs.title: Section 5: Applying the Workflow to Unfamiliar Languages (Questions 18-20)
docs.text:
Question 18: In the Menda project, Second level opens with › (U+203A) and closes with ‹ (U+2039). You accidentally enter ‹ in the Second level Opening cell and › in the Closing cell, then run the check on John. What do you see, and what is the fix? - A) No results; Paratext pairs single guillemets whichever way they point - B) Results only at John 19:21, where Third level reuses « and » - C) Second level results throughout; edit the text so ‹ opens and › closes - D) Second level results throughout; swap the two cells, check the Example

Question 19: Waku uses an em dash — (U+2014) as its First level opening, continuer and closing mark. With Waku correctly configured, the check still reports six "found as a word medial character" results on em dashes that the translation team confirms are parenthetical asides, not speech. What is the right handling? - A) Add a Project Note at each verse, and raise other punctuation for asides with the team - B) Add — (U+2014) to Word-medial punctuation so those dashes are read as part of words - C) Replace the parenthetical em dashes with brackets yourself so the count reaches zero - D) Set every quotation type to Quote marks are optional so the dashes are no longer flagged

Question 20: True or False: Once a project's Quote marks and Quotation types tabs correctly describe the language, the Quotations check run on every book will return zero results. - A) True - B) False
